The ferry put me ashore at Gull Point an hour after dark, and by the time I had climbed the cliff path my hands were raw from the rope rail. The lamp was already turning above me. I could see its long arm sweep over the water, then over the roofs of the cottages, then out to sea again.

My uncle was in the kitchen, mending a net by the fire.

“You’re late, Kit,” said Uncle Abel, without looking up.

“The tide was against me,” I said.

“The tide is always against you.”

“Then I shall have to row harder.”

He laughed at that, a short dry bark, and pushed the lantern across the table towards me.

“Take this up to the gallery. And mind the third step; it’s rotten through.”

“I know about the step.”

“You knew about it last winter, too, and you still came down on your back.”

I did not answer him. I took the lantern and climbed, counting the steps under my breath, and I stepped over the third one with more care than I would have admitted. From the gallery the village looked very small. Somewhere below, a door banged and a woman’s voice called my uncle’s name.

When I came down again Mrs. Pruett was standing in the doorway with a basket on her arm and the wind pulling at her shawl.

“There you are,” she said. “Your uncle has been fretting since noon.”

“He has not,” said Uncle Abel.

“He has,” said Mrs. Pruett. “Tell him he has, my dear.”

“He has,” I agreed.

“Traitor,” muttered my uncle.

Mrs. Pruett set the basket on the table and began to unpack it: a loaf, a pot of plum jam, a parcel of salt fish wrapped in newspaper.

“Davy Rowe came by the shop this morning,” she said. “He swears there’s a ship standing off the point.”

“In this weather?” I asked.

“In this weather. Lying to, with no lights.”

Uncle Abel put down his needle.

“What colours was she flying?”

“Davy couldn’t tell. Too much spray.”

“Then I’ll go and look,” I said, already reaching for my coat.

“You will not,” said my uncle. “Not in the dark, and not alone.”

“Then come with me.”

He looked at me for a long moment, and then at Mrs. Pruett, who only shrugged.

“Your mother was just the same,” he said at last. “Get the other lantern.”

We went out together into the wind. The path to the point runs along the top of the cliff, and in places it is no wider than a man’s shoulders; I kept one hand on my uncle’s sleeve and the other on the lantern, and neither of us spoke until we reached the cairn.

“There,” I said, and pointed.

“I see her.”

“She’s too close. She’ll be on the Teeth by morning.”

“Not if she has any sense.”

“And if she hasn’t?”

My uncle did not answer at once. The ship rode low in the water, a shape blacker than the sea around it, and as we watched a single light flared on her deck and went out.

“Then we wake the village,” he said. “Run, Kit. Ring the bell at the chapel, and don’t stop until every window is lit.”

I ran.
